chapter_summary:
Displays make your projects interactive by showing data, status, and menus. The classic character LCD, often a 16x2 or 20x4 model, displays text using predefined character blocks. Modern versions include an I2C backpack, which reduces the number of wires from many parallel pins to just four: VCC, GND, SDA, and SCL.

Before using I2C devices, you must enable the I2C interface on the Raspberry Pi. Open `raspi-config`, go to Interface Options, select I2C, and enable it. Then reboot. You can check whether devices are detected with the `i2cdetect` command:

```bash
sudo apt install i2c-tools
sudo i2cdetect -y 1
```

This prints a grid showing the addresses of connected I2C devices. A common LCD I2C address is `0x27` or `0x3F`.

In Python, you can use the `lcd1602` or `rpi_lcd` library, or the `gpiozero` `LCD` class if available. Here is an example using `rpi_lcd`:

```python
from rpi_lcd import LCD
from time import sleep

lcd = LCD()
lcd.text("Hello, Pi!", 1)
lcd.text("Cohortia", 2)
sleep(2)
lcd.clear()
```

OLED displays are more flexible than character LCDs. A 0.96-inch monochrome OLED with an SSD1306 driver can display text, shapes, and simple graphics. It also uses I2C, so wiring is simple. The `luma.oled` library is a popular choice:

```bash
pip install luma.oled
```

Example:

```python
from luma.core.interface.serial import i2c
from luma.core.render import canvas
from luma.oled.device import ssd1306
from PIL import ImageFont

serial = i2c(port=1, address=0x3C)
device = ssd1306(serial)

with canvas(device) as draw:
    draw.text((0, 0), "Hello, OLED!", fill="white")
    draw.text((0, 20), "Temp: 23.5 C", fill="white")
```

When displaying sensor data, formatting matters. Floating-point numbers can be hard to read with too many decimal places. Use Python's f-strings to control precision. Clear old text before writing new values to avoid leftover characters on the screen. Update the display only when values change or at a moderate rate to avoid flicker.

screens.title: Displays: Character LCD and OLED
screens.subtitle: Connect, detect, and present sensor data using I2C character LCDs and SSD1306 OLEDs

narration.text: Displays bring your Raspberry Pi projects alive. In this lesson you'll learn how the classic character LCD and the small monochrome OLED differ, how to wire them over I2C, and how to present sensor values clearly. We will cover enabling I2C on the Pi, using i2cdetect to find device addresses, and simple Python workflows to write text, clear old characters, and control update rates. You will see concrete examples: a 16 by 2 text display showing temperature and a 0.96 inch SSD1306 OLED drawing text and simple graphics. I will also explain common pitfalls, like leftover characters when writing shorter strings and flicker from updating too frequently. By the end you'll know which display suits menu-style text versus small graphics, how to install and use the right Python libraries, and how to format floats for readability. Think about a weather sensor: which display would best show quick numeric updates and which one would support a miniature bar graph? That question helps you choose the right display for your project.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Displays let your Pi communicate state, sensor readings, and simple menus. Choosing the right hardware and updating displays sensibly prevents visual glitches and improves usability.

screens.title: Character LCDs: how they work
screens.subtitle: Predefined character blocks, sizes, and what an I2C backpack changes

narration.text: A character LCD displays text using fixed character cells arranged in a grid, commonly 16 by 2 or 20 by 4. Each cell can show a predefined character from the module's character set. The display itself is driven either in parallel or through an I2C backpack, which translates I2C commands into the parallel signals the LCD expects. The backpack reduces wiring to four wires: power, ground, SDA and SCL. That simplification matters when you have limited GPIO pins or many devices on the bus. A concrete example is a 16 by 2 panel showing two lines: a device name and a temperature. Because each cell holds one character, you must manage cursor positions and clearing carefully: writing a shorter string where a longer one previously appeared can leave trailing characters unless you explicitly clear the remainder of the line. A common misconception is that the backpack adds features beyond wiring; in fact it only simplifies connectivity and does not change how characters are stored or displayed. Key practical tips: confirm your display geometry when addressing rows and columns, and test whether your backpack uses a common address like 0x27 or 0x3F before coding. How will you ensure a short string won’t leave old characters behind in your next project?

keyIdea.title: Character LCD essentials
keyIdea.text: 16x2 and 20x4 panels show text in fixed cells; an I2C backpack reduces wiring but you still manage cursor and clearing logic.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › Character LCDs

Fixed character cells arranged in rows and columns. Controlled via parallel pins or an I2C backpack.
Sizes to expect
16×2 for simple status lines; 20×4 for longer menus and more lines of data.
I2C backpack role
Translates I2C commands to the LCD's parallel interface, letting you use SDA and SCL instead of many GPIO lines.
Common misconception
The backpack simplifies wiring but does not change how characters are stored or how cursor addressing works.
Example
Display two lines: device name on line one, and a formatted temperature on line two. Use the cursor to place values precisely and clear trailing characters when updating shorter values.
Key Takeaway

I2C backpacks make wiring simple; you still manage line lengths and cursor updates to keep text clean.

Common Mistake

Writing a shorter string over a longer one without clearing leaves stray characters; always clear or pad lines before updating.

screens.title: Enable I2C and detect devices
screens.subtitle: Raspi-config steps, reboot, and i2cdetect usage

narration.text: Before connecting an I2C display you must enable the I2C interface on the Raspberry Pi. The usual approach is to open the system configuration tool, select interface options, enable I2C, then reboot so the kernel loads the required modules. After reboot, install the I2C tools package if needed, and run the detection utility on the correct bus. The common commands are installing i2c-tools and running the detector against bus one. The detector prints a grid where present devices appear as hex addresses. For example, seeing 27 in the grid means a device responds at address 0x27. That gives you the address to pass into your display library. A frequent beginner mistake is assuming the bus number or forgetting to enable I2C before detection; if nothing appears, verify wiring and that I2C is enabled. Another detail: some devices use 0x3C or 0x3F; check the detector rather than guessing. Practice: enable I2C, reboot, run the detector, and note the address you see. That address is the first piece of information your Python code needs to communicate with the display. Enable I2C and detect devices means enable i2c in raspi-config, reboot, then use i2cdetect to find device addresses like 0x27 or 0x3c.. In practical terms, raspi-config steps, reboot, and i2cdetect usage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: I2C activation
keyIdea.text: Enable I2C in raspi-config, reboot, then use i2cdetect to find device addresses like 0x27 or 0x3C.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › Enable I2C
Step-by-step
  1. Open the Raspberry Pi configuration tool and choose Interface Options.
  2. Select I2C and enable it, then reboot the Pi to load I2C modules.
  3. Install the I2C tools package if missing.
  4. Run the detector on bus one and note addresses shown, e.g., 27 or 3C.
Remember: if no addresses appear, check wiring and the enabled state in the config tool before troubleshooting code.
Detector output
The detector prints a grid. A number like 27 indicates a device at 0x27. Use that address when creating device objects in Python.
Pro Tip

If you have multiple devices, label each by address before coding so you can avoid address conflicts on the bus.

Pitfall

Forgetting to reboot after enabling I2C or using the wrong bus number will make the detector show no devices.

narration.text: There are several ways to drive a character LCD from Python. Simple libraries like rpi_lcd offer a minimal A P I that focuses on writing text to specific lines. Others, such as lcd1602 or wrappers around low-level drivers, provide more control over the cursor, custom characters, and backlight options. If your environment includes higher-level helpers, gpiozero may expose an LCD class that integrates with other gpiozero components. A concrete snippet using rpi_lcd shows how straightforward this is: create an LCD object, call a text method to write a line, pause, and clear the screen. That pattern works well for short status messages. A common misconception is that all libraries behave identically; in practice their APIs differ in method names, argument order, and address handling for I2C backpacks. Before you copy code, confirm the library's expected address parameter and row indexing. Also check whether the library auto-clears the display or expects you to clear between updates. When you try a library for the first time, run a short example to confirm the address and behavior, then embed the same calls in your sensor loop with controlled updates rather than continuous rapid writes.

keyIdea.title: Library choices
keyIdea.text: Different Python libraries vary in API and behavior; test address handling and clearing behavior before integrating into loops.

screens.title: Character LCD vs OLED
screens.subtitle: Text-only cells versus pixel graphics — what each is best for

narration.text: Character LCDs and OLEDs serve overlapping but distinct roles. Character displays are ideal for simple, stable text: device names, short readings, menus, and status lines. They are easy to read at a glance and often inexpensive. OLEDs using SSD1306 are pixel displays, supporting text but also shapes and tiny graphs; they are better for compact graphics like a small bar graph for humidity. A concrete example: a 16 by 2 LCD can show a sensor name and a numeric value clearly, but adding a graph is awkward. An SSD1306 can show the same number and a horizontal bar scaled to percent. A typical misconception is that OLEDs always replace character LCDs; however, character panels can be clearer for fixed textual menus and consume predictable power. When choosing, consider readability, the need for graphics, available libraries, and bus addresses. Also consider update strategy: OLEDs rendered with Pillow and luma. oled let you redraw frames but may need throttling to avoid visible flicker, while character LCDs require careful clearing or padding to maintain clean text. Which format best fits your next project's UI goals?

keyIdea.title: Choose by need
keyIdea.text: Use character LCDs for clear text and predictable layout; use SSD1306 OLEDs when you need tiny graphics or custom rendering.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › LCD vs OLED
Character LCD
  • Best for stable textual menus and status lines.
  • Simple API usage for writing fixed rows of text.
  • Requires cursor and clearing logic when updating values.
Example: 16×2 showing "Room" and "23.5 C" as two lines.
SSD1306 OLED
  • Pixel-based; supports text and simple graphics via Pillow rendering.
  • Good for tiny bar graphs, icons, or more flexible layouts.
  • Redraw strategy affects perceived flicker; throttle updates.
Example: OLED renders "Temp: 23.5 C" and a horizontal humidity bar at 60% width.
Key Takeaway

Pick character LCDs for simple text and OLEDs for small graphics; match update strategy to the display type to avoid flicker.

screens.title: SSD1306 OLED and luma.oled
screens.subtitle: How SSD1306-driven OLEDs render text and graphics using Pillow

narration.text: The SSD1306 driver powers many small monochrome OLEDs you will see in Raspberry Pi projects. These displays speak I2C and present a pixel grid you can draw into using a library such as luma. oled paired with Pillow. The typical flow is: create an I2C serial interface with the appropriate address, instantiate the device object, then use a canvas context to draw text and shapes. Pillow gives you fonts and drawing primitives, so you can render text at chosen coordinates and draw lines, rectangles, or a bar representing sensor values. A concrete example is opening a canvas and writing two text lines, then drawing a filled rectangle whose width maps to humidity percent. A common mistake is updating the OLED too frequently; drawing many frames per second can cause flicker and waste C P U. Throttle updates to a comfortable rate and redraw only when values visibly change. Another misconception is that OLEDs automatically handle text wrapping; you control coordinates and font sizing directly. Try a short code run to confirm your address and test simple text before adding graphics.

keyIdea.title: OLED rendering model
keyIdea.text: SSD1306 offers pixel access; use luma.oled and Pillow to draw text and small graphics, and throttle redraws to avoid flicker.

content.html:

What it does
A pixel-based display driven over I2C. Use luma.oled with Pillow to draw text at coordinates and simple shapes like bars.
Typical pattern
Create an I2C serial with port and address, instantiate device, then draw within a canvas context to render text and shapes.
Example
Open a canvas and write "Hello, OLED!" and a second line with a temperature. Map humidity percent to a rectangle width for a small bar graph.
Pro Tip

Throttle redraws and only update when values change to reduce flicker and CPU load.

Key Takeaway

SSD1306 with luma.oled gives flexible pixel drawing; manage redraw frequency and coordinate placement carefully.

screens.title: Writing to displays with Python
screens.subtitle: Example flows for character LCDs and SSD1306 OLEDs

narration.text: Let's walk through typical Python flows for both display types. For a character LCD you instantiate the library's class, write a string to a specific line, then sleep and clear if needed. That short pattern is ideal for status lines. For example, create an LCD object, call a text method for line one, then a second call for line two, pause, and clear. For an SSD1306 OLED, you create an I2C serial interface with the device address, instantiate the SSD1306 device, and then open a draw canvas. Inside the canvas you call text drawing methods and shape primitives to render a bar or label. A practical tip is to format sensor values before sending them to the display. Use formatted strings to limit decimals — this keeps the output readable. Another important point: avoid continuous rapid writes. Update at a moderate rate, for example every two seconds, or only when a reading changes by a perceptible amount. A common misconception is that printing every sample is harmless — in practice it causes flicker and extra C P U usage. Try these simple flows and then adapt the cadence to your sensor's stability.

keyIdea.title: Typical flows
keyIdea.text: Character LCDs: create, write lines, sleep, clear. OLEDs: setup serial, use canvas to draw text and shapes, and throttle redraws.

Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › Writing in Python
Character LCD flow
Create LCD object, write line one and two, use sleep, then clear when appropriate. Confirm I2C address first.
Example scenario
Show a sensor name on line one and a formatted numeric value on line two, updating every two seconds when the value changes.
OLED flow
Create I2C serial with address, instantiate device, then draw into a canvas context using Pillow text and shapes.
Example scenario
Render a temperature label and a humidity bar whose width maps to percent, then present the composed frame with a controlled update interval.
Key Takeaway

Format values first and throttle updates; these practices prevent flicker and leftover text issues.

Pro Tip

When swapping displays, reuse the same formatted output but adapt rendering calls to the new API.

Common Mistake

Neglecting to clear or pad character lines leads to trails of old characters when values shorten.

screens.title: Format sensor data cleanly
screens.subtitle: Controlling precision, padding, and update frequency

narration.text: Formatting sensor data for readability is essential. Raw floating-point numbers can include many decimals that add noise rather than value. Use formatted strings to control precision — for example round to one decimal place for temperature if that level of detail is meaningful. Another formatting concern for character LCDs is padding: when a new value is shorter than the previous one, trailing characters remain. You can avoid this by clearing the line before writing or writing a fixed-width formatted string padded with spaces. Update frequency also matters: refreshing the display only when the value changes or at a moderate interval, such as every two seconds, reduces visible flicker and lowers processor usage. A concrete practice is to compare the last displayed value with the new reading and only redraw on change beyond a small threshold. A common misconception is that more frequent updates are always better; in reality human perception and stability of many sensors mean slower, controlled updates are clearer. Try limiting precision, using fixed-width fields or explicit clears, and adding an update threshold to your loop. Format sensor data cleanly means limit decimals, pad or clear character lcd lines, and update only when values change or at a sensible interval to prevent flicker.. In practical terms, controlling precision, padding, and update frequency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Formatting rules
keyIdea.text: Limit decimals, pad or clear character LCD lines, and update only when values change or at a sensible interval to prevent flicker.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › Formatting Sensor Data
Control precision
Use formatted strings to limit decimals so numbers are quick to read, for example one decimal for temperature when appropriate.
Padding and clearing
Clear the line before writing or use a fixed-width formatted string padded with spaces to avoid leftover characters on character LCDs.
Update strategy
Only update on meaningful value changes or at a modest rate, for example every two seconds, to reduce flicker and CPU use.
Key Takeaway

Readable displays need controlled precision, careful clearing, and sensible refresh intervals.

Concrete example
Compare last and new readings and only redraw if the change exceeds a small threshold. Format numbers with a fixed precision and pad strings when writing to a fixed-width character display.

screens.title: Swap to OLED and add a bar graph
screens.subtitle: Transition steps and drawing a humidity bar on SSD1306

narration.text: After you confirm your character LCD work, replacing it with an SSD1306 OLED requires just a few changes. First, note the OLED's I2C address from the detector, often 0x3C. Install luma. oled and Pillow if needed. In code, create an I2C serial interface with the correct port and address, then instantiate the SSD1306 device. Use a canvas context to draw text and shapes. For a humidity bar graph draw a filled rectangle whose width is proportional to humidity percentage. For example map 0–100 percent to 0–display-width pixels and draw the rectangle starting at a small left margin. Render the temperature as text above or beside the bar. Redraw only when the reading changes beyond a threshold or at a moderate interval to avoid visible flicker. A common misconception is that drawing a bar requires complex graphics code — a single filled rectangle often suffices for small indicators. Test your mapping with known values to verify the bar scales correctly. After drawing, consider whether a thin border or label improves readability. This transition demonstrates how the same sensor data can be rendered differently to enhance clarity.

keyIdea.title: OLED transition
keyIdea.text: Swap libraries, create a canvas, and draw a bar scaled to humidity percent; throttle redraws to avoid flicker.

Module 05 › Chapter 5.3 › OLED Bar Graph

  • Install luma.oled and Pillow and create an I2C serial for the address.
  • Instantiate the SSD1306 device and draw within a canvas using text and rectangle primitives.
Bar mapping
Map humidity percent to pixel width. For example, percent divided by 100 times available pixel width yields the rectangle width for a filled bar.
Example
Draw "Temp: 23.5 C" and below it a humidity bar scaled to percent. Use a left margin and a thin border for clarity.
Key Takeaway

A single rectangle scaled to percent creates an effective mini bar graph for OLED displays.

screens.title: Interpreting i2cdetect output
screens.subtitle: What a detected address means and how to use it

narration.text: Understanding the i2cdetect grid is a small but important assessment. When you run the detector and see a number such as 27 appear in the grid it means a device answered at the hexadecimal address 0x27. That address is what your display library will use when creating a device object. If no addresses appear, either I2C is not enabled, the wiring is incorrect, or the device uses a different bus number. A practical question for assessment is: you run the detector and see 27 — what does that mean? The correct answer is that a device is present at 0x27 and you should use that address in your code. A common misconception is to treat the detector output as a port number — it is not; it is the device address on the I2C bus. In lab checks, repeat detection after each wiring change to confirm the device continues to respond. This habit saves debugging time when you switch displays or add sensors to the same bus. Interpreting i2cdetect output means a number in i2cdetect is the device's i2c address; use it when instantiating display or sensor objects in python.. In practical terms, what a detected address means and how to use it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Detector interpretation
keyIdea.text: A number in i2cdetect is the device's I2C address; use it when instantiating display or sensor objects in Python.

What the grid shows
Hex addresses for devices that responded on the I2C bus; for example 27 corresponds to 0x27.

  • Verify wiring and bus number if no devices show.
  • Re-run after changes to confirm the device still appears.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three concise reminders to carry forward

narration.text: Keep three core ideas in mind. First, enabling I2C and using i2cdetect to find addresses is your first step before writing any code. Second, choose the display type that fits the UI: character LCDs for stable text and SSD1306 OLEDs for small graphics. Third, format and update sensibly: limit decimals, clear or pad character lines, and refresh only when needed to avoid leftover text and flicker. Practicing these steps by wiring a 16 by 2 to show temperature, then swapping to an OLED for a humidity bar, will cement these concepts. Ask yourself as you design: which display will make my data easiest to read and how often does it need to update? That simple question guides the choices you make in real projects.
